edition.fomc: Next: 9–10 Dec (25bp hike ~99%; multiple Fed officials flagged urgency; Waller suggested large hike may be needed; labour data the swing factor for 50bp)
edition.stripNote: Sat 21 Nov. Friday's session was dominated by one of the year's sharpest risk-off sell-offs. The Dow and S&P 500 entered correction territory; the Nasdaq plunged into its third correction of 2026, wiping out its gains for the year. AI stocks led the decline despite Anthropic's (ANT) strong Thursday debut. Gold fell for a tenth consecutive session to $3,560, a 14-month low, as Fed rate-hike odds hit 99% and the dollar surged. Silver crashed 6.6% to $41.50. Brent crude slid 1.8% to $90.33; WTI fell to $81.50 — oil heading for a third straight weekly decline as Middle East exports recover despite continued Hormuz attacks. A tanker was hit by a projectile in the Strait on Friday, the seventh strike in a week — JMIC rates the threat as severe. Combined traffic 65% below pre-conflict levels. Copper dropped 2.5% to $5.47/lb; platinum fell 3.9% to $1,295; palladium dropped 2.3% to $895. Coal held at $150. Bitcoin plunged below $60,000 to ~$58,200, down 8.8%; Ethereum crashed to $1,597. Corn hit a 4-month low at 434½¢; wheat dipped to 574¼¢; soybeans rose 1.1% to 1,220¾¢. Cocoa rebounded 2.4% to $5,294. LME base metals weaker: nickel ~$15,400, zinc ~$3,490, tin ~$42,050. November 27 gallium/germanium/antimony deadline now 6 days away — no extension announced. G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro this weekend.

overview: Friday's session saw one of the year's sharpest risk-off sell-offs sweep across global markets. The Dow and S&P 500 entered correction territory while the Nasdaq plunged into its third correction of 2026, wiping out its gains for the year — a brutal semiconductor sell-off led by AMD and Micron dragged AI stocks lower despite Anthropic's (ANT) strong Thursday debut. Gold fell for a tenth consecutive session to approximately $3,560 per ounce, a 14-month low, as Fed rate-hike odds for December hit 99% and the dollar surged to its strongest level in 19 months. Silver crashed 6.6% to $41.50. Brent crude slid 1.8% to $90.33 per barrel despite a fresh tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz — recovering Middle East export flows offset the geopolitical premium, pushing oil toward its third straight weekly decline. WTI fell to $81.50. Copper dropped 2.5% to $5.47 per pound. Platinum fell 3.9% to $1,295; palladium dropped 2.3% to $895. Newcastle coal held at $150. Corn hit a 4-month low at 434½ cents; wheat dipped to 574¼ cents; soybeans bucked the trend, rising 1.1% to 1,220¾ cents as bargain buying emerged.

Bitcoin plunged below $60,000 to approximately $58,200, falling 8.8% as the equity rout spread to crypto. Ethereum crashed 11.4% to $1,597; spot Bitcoin ETF outflows have now exceeded $2.5 billion in 2026. The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October — a tanker was hit by a projectile near Khasab, Oman on Friday, the seventh strike in the region in a week. Combined Hormuz traffic stands at about 65% below pre-conflict levels. JMIC rates the threat as severe with further deliberate attacks highly likely. Despite the sustained attacks, oil prices were heading for a third straight weekly decline as Middle East crude exports returned toward pre-war levels. Cocoa rebounded 2.4% to $5,294 on West African supply concerns. LME base metals were broadly weaker: nickel fell to approximately $15,400, zinc dropped to $3,490, and tin declined to $42,050. The November 27 deadline for China's export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony is now 6 days away with no extension announced — the G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro this weekend provides a last venue for bilateral discussions before the deadline.

watchItems.title: November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline now 6 days away — no extension announced
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline for China's US-specific export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony is now 6 days away. Neither the trilateral summit nor any subsequent diplomatic channel has produced progress on critical minerals. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium, 60–80% of germanium, and close to half of mined antimony. Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus approximately $460 domestically — a roughly 4.5x premium. The G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro this weekend provides a final major diplomatic venue for bilateral discussions. If the bans resume next week, Western semiconductor and defence supply chains face renewed disruption. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery has taken FID but is not yet producing.

watchItems.title: G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro — last major diplomatic venue before November 27 deadline
watchItems.text: The G20 summit convenes in Rio de Janeiro this weekend (November 21–22), providing a critical venue for bilateral sidelines on Hormuz, trade policy and critical minerals. The trilateral summit in Shenzhen earlier this week produced a symbolic peace declaration but no concrete deliverables. With the November 27 gallium deadline 6 days away, any progress at the G20 on critical minerals could shift the trajectory. On Hormuz, the gap between recovering Middle East export flows and surging tanker attacks presents a complex diplomatic challenge. Any Hormuz ceasefire framework would have immediate implications for energy, sulfur and helium markets.

watchItems.title: Hormuz escalation — most active week since mid-October; 7 strikes on 6 vessels; traffic 65% below pre-conflict
watchItems.text: The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October. A tanker was hit by a projectile near Khasab, Oman on Friday — the seventh strike in the region in a week according to Orbital Risk Intelligence. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, with two seafarers missing and 13 injured. Combined Hormuz traffic is about 65% below pre-conflict levels. JMIC rates the threat as severe. The paradox is that oil prices are falling despite the attacks — Middle East crude exports have returned toward pre-war levels, suggesting the southern corridor is functioning despite the operational risks. The US is widening its blockade of Iranian ship-to-ship oil transfers.

watchItems.title: Market correction deepens — Dow, S&P enter correction; Nasdaq's third of 2026; crypto below $60K
watchItems.text: Friday's sell-off pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory for the first time since the onset of the Hormuz crisis, while the Nasdaq entered its third correction of 2026. AI stocks led the decline despite Anthropic's strong Thursday IPO debut. Gold's tenth consecutive daily decline and Bitcoin's plunge below $60,000 suggest the risk-off positioning is broadening beyond equities. Fed rate-hike odds at 99% for December, the dollar at 19-month highs and Treasury yields near 5.10% are creating a hostile environment for all risk assets. The key question is whether the G20 summit or any shift in the Fed narrative can arrest the sell-off before it deepens further.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: 10th consecutive decline · 14-month low · down ~8% on the week — worst in 8 months · 10Y yield ~5.10% · dollar at 19-month high · Dec hike odds 99%
desk.sum: Gold fell for a tenth consecutive session on Friday, dropping approximately 2.4% to $3,560 per ounce — a 14-month low and the longest losing streak in over a year. The relentless selling accelerated as CME FedWatch showed December rate-hike odds hitting 99%, the dollar surged to its strongest level in 19 months, and the 10-year Treasury yield pushed toward 5.10%. The intraday low of $3,513 marks the weakest level since September 2025. The sell-off is part of a broader risk-off liquidation that sent the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory. Gold is down approximately 8% on the week — its worst weekly performance in eight months. Key support at $3,500.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Crashed · gold-silver ratio ~86 · down ~28% over past month · first dip below $42 since early 2026 · industrial exposure amplified sell-off
desk.sum: Silver crashed 6.6% to $41.50 per ounce on Friday, one of the worst-performing commodities of the session. The intraday low reached $40.99 — the first dip below $41 in months. Silver's dual precious-industrial profile made it especially vulnerable as both yield-driven precious metal selling and risk-off industrial demand concerns compounded. The gold-silver ratio widened to approximately 86. Silver is down roughly 28% over the past month, with the sell-off accelerating as December rate-hike odds hit 99% and the Nasdaq entered correction territory. The break below $42 opens support at $40–$41.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $81.50 · third straight weekly decline · ME exports recovering to pre-war levels · tanker hit in Hormuz Fri · intraday high $92.22 · supply surplus fears
desk.sum: Brent crude fell 1.8% to $90.33 per barrel on Friday despite a fresh tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz — recovering Middle East export flows offset the geopolitical premium. The US maritime agency warned that Hormuz shipments had returned to roughly pre-war levels, adding to supply pressure. WTI fell to approximately $81.50. Oil is heading for a third straight weekly decline, down roughly 6% on the week. The intraday range was wide: Brent touched $92.22 before sellers took control. The paradox of falling oil prices amid surging Hormuz attacks reflects the market's view that crude export flows are normalising despite the operational risks.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$12,060/t · continued losses · dollar at 19-month high · DRC logistics disruption ongoing · Chinese physical premiums at records
desk.sum: Copper fell 2.5% to $5.47 per pound (approximately $12,060 per tonne LME) on Friday, extending losses in the broader risk-off sell-off. The dollar at 19-month highs remains the dominant headwind. Chinese physical premiums have hit record levels even as LME prices decline, signalling divergence between financial and physical markets. The DRC bridge collapse continues to disrupt logistics. AI data-centre, EV and electrification demand remain structural long-term drivers, but the hostile macro environment caps near-term upside. Key support at $5.40 per pound ($11,900 per tonne).

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up ~40% YTD · held steady again · winter demand · LNG supply crisis continues · no Hormuz deal · Indonesia coal ~$145
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held at $150 per tonne on Friday, continuing to buck broader commodity weakness as winter demand and the Hormuz-driven LNG supply crisis sustain the thermal fuel bid. Coal is up approximately 40% year to date. The G20 summit this weekend provides another venue for Hormuz discussions but expectations are low. QatarEnergy's force majeure continues through at least end-December 2026. Indonesian coal trades near $145 as mining demand builds. The energy supply crisis and coal-to-gas substitution dynamics remain supportive through winter.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Sharp decline · sold off with broader precious metals · EV shift weighing · South African supply constrained · yields headwind
desk.sum: Platinum fell 3.9% to $1,295 per ounce on Friday, caught in the broad precious metals sell-off. The EV transition continues to pressure automotive catalyst demand. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues. With the dollar at a 19-month high, December rate-hike odds at 99% and Treasury yields near 5.10%, the macro environment is increasingly hostile. Platinum has now lost approximately 7.5% over two sessions. Hydrogen electrolysis demand provides a structural long-term floor but cannot offset near-term selling pressure.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Deep below $900 · down ~35% YoY · EV transition headwind dominant · weakest sustained level since 2018
desk.sum: Palladium fell 2.3% to $895 per ounce on Friday, dropping below $900 for the first time since 2018. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — continues to dominate. With the dollar at 19-month highs, yields near 5.10% and December rate-hike odds at 99%, the macro environment remains hostile. Tight South African mine supply offers limited support. The break below $900 is technically significant and opens the next support zone around $870–$880.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: Tanker hit by projectile Fri · 7 strikes on 6 vessels in past week · traffic 65% below pre-conflict · JMIC threat: SEVERE · 3 US carriers in Gulf · exports recovering despite attacks
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October. A tanker was hit by a projectile near Khasab, Oman on Friday at 1500 UTC — the seventh strike in the region in a week. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, with two seafarers missing and 13 injured. JMIC rates the threat as severe with further deliberate attacks highly likely. Combined Hormuz traffic is about 65% below pre-conflict levels. The paradox: despite surging attacks, Middle East crude exports have returned toward pre-war levels according to the US maritime agency, pushing oil prices lower. The US is widening its blockade of Iranian ship-to-ship transfers. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Hit 4-month low · down 11¢ on the week · dollar strength persists · South American planting favourable
desk.sum: December corn fell 4½ cents to 434½ cents per bushel on Friday, hitting a 4-month low as dollar strength continued to weigh on US export competitiveness. Corn is down 11 cents on the week. The broader risk-off sell-off added to pressure across agricultural commodities. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the November WASDE report provides a structural floor. The November 27 critical minerals deadline adds geopolitical uncertainty. Key support at 430 cents.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Continued decline · down 19¢ on the week · SovEcon Russia estimate supports floor · export demand picking up at lower levels
desk.sum: December SRW wheat fell 4 cents to 574¼ cents per bushel on Friday, extending the week's decline. Wheat is down 19 cents on the week. HRW wheat fell 1¼ cents to 624½ cents. The sell-off was broad-based amid the risk-off environment. SovEcon's Russian wheat export estimate of 36 million tonnes — below the USDA's forecast — provides a structural floor. Export demand continues to pick up at the depressed price levels. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for US competitiveness.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month ~$12.21 · rebounded · down 10¾¢ on the week · summit no Busan progress · South American supply competitive
desk.sum: January soybeans rose 13¼ cents to 1,220¾ cents per bushel on Friday, one of the few commodities to end the session higher as bargain buying emerged after the week's heavy selling. Soybeans are still down 10¾ cents on the week. The trilateral summit produced no visible progress on the Busan truce soybean commitments. South American supplies remain more competitive at current exchange rates. The G20 summit this weekend provides another venue for trade discussions. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for US exports.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,597 · plunged below $60K · Nasdaq enters correction · spot ETF outflows >$2.5B in 2026 · Fear & Greed deep Extreme Fear
desk.sum: Bitcoin plunged below $60,000 to approximately $58,200 on Friday, falling 8.8% as the broader equity sell-off spread to crypto. The Nasdaq entering its third correction of 2026 triggered widespread risk-off positioning. Ethereum crashed 11.4% to $1,597. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows have now exceeded $2.5 billion in 2026, with IBIT down 5.9% and ETHA down 9.2% on the day. The Fear and Greed Index remains deep in Extreme Fear territory. Key levels to watch: BTC reclaiming $60,000 and ETH recovering above $1,800. The macro headwinds from the FOMC remain dominant, with December rate-hike odds at 99%.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM Dec contract ~$29 · TTF ~$29.50 · HH ~$3.35 · QatarEnergy FM continues · EU storage 70.8% — 20% below 5Y avg · oil slide easing LNG premium
desk.sum: The Asian LNG spot JKM December contract trades near $29 per MMBtu, up from the $27.50 rollover level as winter demand supports. TTF sits near $29.50 per MMBtu; Henry Hub near $3.35. EU gas storage at 70.8% is 20% below the five-year average heading into winter — the thinnest in a decade. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026. Despite oil's slide on recovering Middle East exports, LNG fundamentals remain structurally tight with over 60 bcm of Qatari and UAE loadings lost between March and October. US LNG export feedgas hit a record 19.3 bcf per day.
desk.src: S&P Global Platts · Global LNG Hub · JOGMEC

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · 3 carriers in Gulf · tanker hit Fri · 7 strikes in a week · 6 days to Nov 27 deadline · oil slide easing some supply pressure
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October, with a tanker hit on Friday — the seventh strike in a week. Despite the sustained attacks, Middle East crude exports are recovering toward pre-war levels, which may gradually ease sulfur supply logistics. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). The November 27 export-control deadline is now 6 days away. The G20 summit this weekend provides another diplomatic venue but expectations for supply normalisation remain low.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · G20 this weekend · wheat & corn weakness weighing on fertiliser sentiment
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Wheat and corn both declining on the week, with corn at a 4-month low, is modestly negative for near-term fertiliser demand sentiment. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The G20 summit this weekend provides another venue for trade discussions.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 6 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · no progress from summit or any diplomatic channel · ban resumption increasingly priced in
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The November 27 deadline is now 6 days away with no extension announced. Neither the trilateral summit nor any subsequent diplomatic channel has produced visible progress on critical minerals. Market participants are increasingly pricing in ban resumption. If the deadline passes without extension, overseas prices could spike further. China produces close to half of global mined antimony. The G20 this weekend is a last-chance venue for bilateral discussions.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 6 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · no progress from any diplomatic channel · ban resumption increasingly priced in
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium. The November 27 deadline is now 6 days away with no extension announced from any diplomatic channel. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium and 60–80% of germanium. The underlying licensing regimes remain in force during the suspension. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery has taken FID but is not yet producing. The G20 this weekend provides a final diplomatic venue. Ban resumption is increasingly priced in.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Steady at $5.30 · upstream tightness · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ · Nov 27 deadline 6 days
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, supported by persistent upstream tightness. The November 27 deadline, now 6 days away, affects the broader critical minerals complex. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. The G20 summit this weekend provides a final venue for critical mineral discussions.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Rebounded 2.4% · up from $5,063 on Thu · West African supply concerns reasserted · El Niño risk · $5,000 holding as support
desk.sum: ICE cocoa rebounded 2.4% to $5,294 per tonne on Friday, bucking the broader commodity sell-off as West African supply concerns reasserted themselves. The bounce from $5,063 on Thursday confirms the $5,000 level as strong psychological support. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projection that 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an exceptionally strong El Niño event continues to provide a medium-term bullish underpinning. Despite ICE warehouse inventories at a 2.5-year high of 3.8 million bags, the market remains focused on forward supply risks.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Continued decline from $33,525 · European demand concerns persist · Rotterdam $16–17/lb · DRC bridge disruption ongoing · NMC-to-LFP shift weighing
desk.sum: Cobalt is estimated near $33,000 per tonne, continuing to decline as European demand concerns persist per Argus Media. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $16–17 per pound. The DRC bridge collapse continues to have secondary effects on cobalt logistics, with alternative routes adding time and cost. The NMC-to-LFP battery chemistry shift weighs on the structural demand outlook. The dollar at 19-month highs adds to the headwinds for an already-weak market. The broader risk-off sell-off on Friday further dampened industrial metals sentiment.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Continued decline · InfoLink reports 7.2% fall in Nov · structural oversupply persists · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate continues to decline, estimated near ¥88,000 per tonne. InfoLink reported a 7.2% fall in lithium carbonate prices in early November, driven by expected mine supply recovery and weaker residential demand. Structural oversupply remains the dominant theme, with Goldman Sachs projecting a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Supply ramp-ups in Australia and South America continue to outpace demand growth. The ¥85,000 zone represents next major support.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil slide pressures synthetic costs lower
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight, with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Friday's oil slide to $90.33 modestly reduces synthetic rubber production costs, tilting the balance slightly. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The dollar at 19-month highs remains a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot held above $90 · term price $98/lb near record · IAEA: 78 reactors under construction · miners sliding 23% while prices hold · AI demand structural
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds at $91.55 per pound U₃O₈ as of late October, with long-term contract prices at $98 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. Despite spot prices holding above $90, uranium miners (URNM ETF) have slid approximately 23% year to date, reflecting rate sensitivity, contract-price lag and ETF-driven selling. The IAEA counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide. Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant delays continue to limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: Down ~2.6% in Nov · ex-China NdPr slipping below $110/kg · Nov 27 deadline 6 days · prices fell sharply on Nov 20 sell-off
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide has declined approximately 2.6% in November to around $71 per kilogram domestically in China. SMM reported that prices fell sharply on November 20 amid broader market selling. Ex-China NdPr prices are slipping below the $110 per kilogram support level as oversupply builds. The November 27 US-specific deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony — now 6 days away — adds uncertainty to the broader critical minerals complex. Downstream magnetic material orders remain weak and buyers are cautious about high-priced inventory.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat · broader metals sell-off weighing
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners continue holding a firm pricing stance. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption and the broader commodity sell-off cap near-term gains. Friday's risk-off environment had no direct impact on manganese pricing but adds to the bearish sentiment for industrial metals.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Continued losses · down from $15,665 · Indonesian RKAB uncertainty persists · global surplus continues · macro headwinds dominant
desk.sum: LME nickel fell approximately 1.7% to $15,400 per tonne on Friday, extending losses as the broader macro headwinds reasserted in the risk-off sell-off. Indonesian RKAB mining quota uncertainty persists — potential tightening provides a floor while the global nickel surplus from Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions caps upside. The dollar at 19-month highs remains the primary headwind. The Dow and S&P 500 entering correction territory added to the negative sentiment across industrial metals. Key support at $15,000.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Continued decline · LME backwardation wide · Myanmar ban constraining supply · macro sell-off dominant · cancelled warrants elevated
desk.sum: LME tin fell approximately 3.3% to around $42,050 per tonne on Friday, continuing the sharp sell-off across base metals. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. The LME backwardation remains wide, signalling tight near-term supply. However, macro pressure from the strong dollar, rising yields and the broader equity correction continues to overwhelm supply-side support. The November 27 deadline adds geopolitical uncertainty to the broader metals complex.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: 5-day losing streak extends · TCs deeply negative · structural deficit intact · Chinese smelter restarts · macro headwinds dominant
desk.sum: LME zinc fell approximately 2.0% to $3,490 per tonne on Friday, extending a five-day losing streak amid the broad risk-off sell-off. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments outside China. The structural supply deficit remains intact despite near-term macro pressure. Zinc is still up approximately 15% year-over-year. The dollar at 19-month highs remains the primary headwind. The Dow and S&P 500 entering correction territory added to the negative industrial metals sentiment.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,750 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 6 days to Nov 27 deadline · no progress from any diplomatic channel
desk.sum: European tungsten APT holds at $2,750 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu — Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. The November 27 deadline is now 6 days away with no extension announced. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls. The G20 summit this weekend provides a final venue for bilateral discussions. If the bans resume next week, the Western premium could widen further. The broader risk-off sell-off has not directly impacted tungsten pricing.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · 7 Hormuz strikes in past week · tanker hit Fri · exports recovering but attacks surging
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October — a tanker was hit on Friday, the seventh strike in a week. Despite the sustained attacks, Middle East crude exports are recovering toward pre-war levels, though helium supply logistics from Qatar remain disrupted. QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility repairs remain estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. The G20 provides another diplomatic window but expectations are low.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · corn & wheat weakness negative for fertiliser demand
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Corn hitting a 4-month low and wheat's continued decline are modestly negative for near-term fertiliser demand sentiment. The Hormuz crisis and Friday's fresh tanker attack further reduce the probability of Middle Eastern sulfur supply normalising, keeping the cost structure elevated.
